Q — Explain Rawls’ ‘justice as fairness’ — the original position, veil of ignorance, primary goods, maximin, the two principles and lexical order, the difference principle and democratic equality. Is it both contractual and distributive? (UPSC 2013/2015/2017/2018/2021)
Rawls asks: what rules of justice would free, rational people choose if they did not know their own place in society?
Behind a ‘veil of ignorance’ (not knowing if you’ll be rich or poor) people play safe (maximin) and pick fair rules.
They choose 2 principles in order: (1) equal basic liberty for all; (2) fair equality of opportunity + the ‘difference principle’ (inequalities allowed only if they help the worst-off).
It is contractual (a hypothetical agreement) AND distributive (it shares primary goods to protect the least advantaged).

Q — Make a comparative assessment of the Greek (Plato and Aristotle) perspective of justice with the Rawlsian concept of justice. (UPSC 2020)
Greek justice is about each person keeping to their natural station and getting their ‘due’ — it accepts natural inequality.
Plato: justice = each class doing its own duty (rulers rule, soldiers guard, producers produce); Aristotle: ‘treat equals equally and unequals unequally’.
Rawls: justice = fairness chosen behind a veil of ignorance, giving equal liberty + help to the worst-off.
So Greeks justify hierarchy (functional/proportional), while Rawls builds an egalitarian, individual-rights-based justice.
Both the Greeks and Rawls treat justice as ‘the first virtue of social institutions’, but they differ sharply on its content.
: “each element in society doing its appropriate task, doing it well and doing it only” — every person remaining ‘at the station allotted by nature’, so that reason (the philosopher-kings) rules.
: “treating equals equally and unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities,” dividing it into distributive, corrective and commutative justice.
— Plato’s ‘myth of the metals’, Aristotle’s defence of slavery and the exclusion of women and slaves from the Polis. Justice for them preserves an ordered hierarchy of function and desert.
. Justice is not a fixed natural order but
— the principles that rational people would choose behind a veil of ignorance: equal basic liberty for all, and inequalities permitted only where they benefit the
. Where the Greeks justify inequality, Rawls justifies it only when it uplifts the worst-off.

The Greek view is teleological and community-centred (justice as fitting into a natural whole); the Rawlsian view is individualist and egalitarian (justice as protecting each person’s inviolable rights). Yet both share the conviction that a stable society must rest on justice — and modern affirmative action, echoing Aristotle’s ‘unequals treated unequally’, shows the two traditions are not wholly opposed.

Q — Critically examine Nozick’s libertarian entitlement theory of justice as a critique of Rawls.
Nozick says justice is about how you got your holdings, not about a fair ‘pattern’ of distribution.
If you acquired, transferred or were compensated fairly, you are entitled to keep everything — taxing it for the poor is ‘forced labour’.
So the state must be minimal (a ‘night-watchman’), doing only protection, not redistribution.
Critique: it makes the welfare of the poor depend on the goodwill of the rich; it is a critique of Rawls, not a fuller theory.

The theory ‘makes the welfare of the poor dependent on the justice of the rich’ and effectively defends existing oppression in the name of justice; it ignores that ‘what a person possesses is not due to talent alone’ but also to chance. The text itself judges it “just a criticism of Rawls from a libertarian point of view — not a sound theory in comparison to Rawls.”

Nozick powerfully defends liberty and property against Rawlsian redistribution, but by reducing the state to a guardian of holdings he leaves the disadvantaged at the mercy of the market — which is why his theory is read more as a foil to Rawls than as a self-standing account of justice.
Q — Analyse Amartya Sen’s methodological critique of Rawls — social choice vs rational choice, Niti vs Nyaya, and the realization/capability approach.
Sen accepts Rawls’ goal but rejects his method: real justice can’t be worked out by abstract people in an imaginary situation.
He prefers ‘social choice’ (real people, real situations) over Rawls’ ‘rational choice’.
Niti (perfect just institutions) vs Nyaya (justice as actually realised in people’s lives) — Nyaya matters more.
So focus on removing real injustice and building people’s capabilities, not on designing a perfect blueprint.

Sen does not overthrow Rawls so much as reorient him — from ideal institutions to real lives, from arrangement to realisation. His critique makes justice comparative and practical, better suited to a diverse world where perfectly just institutions may never be agreed upon.
Q — Discuss the types and dimensions of justice — distributive (David Miller), procedural vs substantive, retributive, and social/political/economic/legal. (UPSC 2018)
Justice comes in several forms depending on what is being shared or corrected.
Distributive justice = fair sharing of resources; David Miller gives 3 principles — rights, desert, and need (need is the most appropriate).
Procedural justice = follow fair rules (‘procedure established by law’); substantive justice = a fair outcome (‘due process’).
Justice takes different forms depending on what is being distributed, corrected or enforced.

These dimensions are interlocking: legal and political justice supply the framework, while distributive and substantive justice supply the content — and the modern welfare state, guided by Rawls and Sen, tilts the balance from mere procedure toward substantive, need-based justice.
Q — “Justice is an architectonic and dynamic idea.” Discuss its importance in political philosophy and how conceptions of justice have evolved.
Justice is the ‘first virtue of social institutions’ (Rawls) — the master value the whole of political philosophy revolves around.

‘Dynamic’ = our idea of justice keeps changing — slavery, untouchability and women’s subordination were once ‘justified’, now rejected.
It evolved from Plato/Aristotle → Hobbes → utilitarians → Marxists → today’s affirmative-action redistribution.

Master Questions Q — Explain Rawls’ ‘justice as fairness’ — the original position, veil of ignorance, primary goods, maximin, the two principles and lexical order, the difference principle and democratic equality. Reacting against  utilitarianism  (which can sacrifice the individual for the ‘greatest happiness’), he revives the  Kantian  tradition of human dignity, calling his theory  deontological : “each person possesses an inviolability founded on justice that even the welfare of society cannot override.” The device.  In the  original position  — a hypothetical, purely procedural ‘thought experiment’ — rational, mutually disinterested agents choose principles behind a  veil of ignorance : they do not know their class, race, sex or talents, only that they could be anyone. Being risk-averse they follow the  maximin  rule — choose the option whose worst outcome is best — designing a society acceptable even if ‘your enemy assigns you your place’. The principles  (governing the distribution of  primary goods  — liberty, rights, income, wealth, self-respect): (1) each person has an  equal right to the most extensive basic liberty  compatible with the like liberty of all; (2) social and economic inequalities must be attached to (a) positions open under  fair equality of opportunity  and (b) the  greatest benefit of the least advantaged  — the  difference principle . The rich accept this as their rational choice/social insurance behind the veil; the difference principle is ‘the best possible utilisation of inequality’, unlike socialism’s ‘equal poverty’. Conclusion.  The theory is both  contractual  (a hypothetical agreement reviving Locke, Rousseau and Kant)  and distributive  (it redistributes primary goods to secure the least advantaged) — which is precisely how Rawls ‘enriched’ liberalism by wedding liberty to social equality. As  Nozick  conceded, philosophers must now “either work within Rawls’ theory or explain why not.” Q — Make a comparative assessment of the Greek (Plato and Aristotle) perspective of justice with the Rawlsian concept of justice. (UPSC 2020) Gist — the spine to recall Greek justice is about each person keeping to their natural station and getting their ‘due’ — it accepts natural inequality. Plato: justice = each class doing its own duty (rulers rule, soldiers guard, producers produce); Aristotle: ‘treat equals equally and unequals unequally’. Rawls: justice = fairness chosen behind a veil of ignorance, giving equal liberty + help to the worst-off. So Greeks justify hierarchy (functional/proportional), while Rawls builds an egalitarian, individual-rights-based justice. Model Answer Both the Greeks and Rawls treat justice as ‘the first virtue of social institutions’, but they differ sharply on its content. Plato  (in  The Republic , subtitled ‘concerning justice’) defines justice as  functional harmony : “each element in society doing its appropriate task, doing it well and doing it only” — every person remaining ‘at the station allotted by nature’, so that reason (the philosopher-kings) rules.  Aristotle  makes justice  proportional : “treating equals equally and unequals unequally in proportion to their inequalities,” dividing it into distributive, corrective and commutative justice. Both Greek thinkers therefore accept  natural inequality  — Plato’s ‘myth of the metals’, Aristotle’s defence of slavery and the exclusion of women and slaves from the Polis. Justice for them preserves an ordered hierarchy of function and desert. Rawls , by contrast, starts from the  free and equal individual . Justice is not a fixed natural order but  fairness  — the principles that rational people would choose behind a veil of ignorance: equal basic liberty for all, and inequalities permitted only where they benefit the  least advantaged . Where the Greeks justify inequality, Rawls justifies it only when it uplifts the worst-off. Assessment.  The Greek view is teleological and community-centred (justice as fitting into a natural whole); the Rawlsian view is individualist and egalitarian (justice as protecting each person’s inviolable rights). Yet both share the conviction that a stable society must rest on justice — and modern affirmative action, echoing Aristotle’s ‘unequals treated unequally’, shows the two traditions are not wholly opposed. Q — Examine the communitarian critique of Rawls and assess his response in Political Liberalism. (UPSC 2019) Gist — the spine to recall Communitarians say Rawls’ ‘person behind the veil’ is unreal — a bare individual with no community, history or identity. Real people are a ‘situated self’ shaped by their society; so there can be no single, universal principle of justice. Sandel, Walzer, Taylor, MacIntyre: ‘justice is not the science of homogenisation but the art of differentiation’ (Walzer’s ‘complex equality’). Rawls replies (Political Liberalism): he limits his theory to political institutions and grounds stability in an ‘overlapping consensus’. Model Answer Communitarianism is a reaction against liberalism’s stress on the  autonomous, unencumbered self . Its core claim is that the real person is a  ‘situated (embedded) self’  — “we never look at reality with naked eyes; we always wear the glasses of community.” The self is not prior to its ends but  constituted by them . Michael Sandel  ( Liberalism and the Limits of Justice ) attacks Rawls’ ‘conception of the self’: strip away all a person’s desires, roles and attachments behind the veil and “is anything left of the person?” — the Rawlsian self is ‘woefully impoverished’.  Michael Walzer  ( Spheres of Justice ) argues justice is plural: “different goods ought to be distributed differently, for different reasons, by different agents” — his  complex equality . Charles Taylor  faults Rawls’ ‘atomistic’ individual, insisting the individual’s well-being depends on the good of the community;  Alasdair MacIntyre  holds that people ‘flourish only within socially established cooperative activity’. The shared theme: there is no universal justice — “what is rational in the USA may not be rational in Afghanistan.” Rawls’ response  ( Political Liberalism ): he accommodates the critique without changing his principles. He  limits their scope to political institutions  — a ‘political, not metaphysical’ conception of justice — and grounds stability in an  overlapping consensus : people holding different comprehensive doctrines (Christianity, Islam, liberalism) can still converge on the same political principles for their own reasons, unlike a mere Hobbesian  modus vivendi . This rests on public reason, reciprocity and toleration (the ‘burdens of judgement’). Conclusion.  The communitarians rightly expose the thinness of the abstract self, but Rawls’ political turn shows his liberalism can coexist with cultural diversity — justice as fairness survives as the shared political framework of a plural society, even if not as a universal metaphysics. Q — Critically examine Nozick’s libertarian entitlement theory of justice as a critique of Rawls. Gist — the spine to recall Nozick says justice is about how you got your holdings, not about a fair ‘pattern’ of distribution. If you acquired, transferred or were compensated fairly, you are entitled to keep everything — taxing it for the poor is ‘forced labour’. So the state must be minimal (a ‘night-watchman’), doing only protection, not redistribution. Critique: it makes the welfare of the poor depend on the goodwill of the rich; it is a critique of Rawls, not a fuller theory. Model Answer Nozick, in  Anarchy, State and Utopia , offers the  entitlement theory  as a libertarian answer to Rawls. Justice is  historical, not patterned : a distribution is just if it arose through just steps, regardless of the resulting shape. He charges that Rawls “compromises liberty for the sake of equality” and violates human dignity. Three principles of entitlement : (1)  just acquisition  — first appropriation so long as no one is made worse off; (2)  just transfer  — voluntary exchange, treating the person as an end (a Kantian point); and (3)  rectification  of past injustice. If holdings pass these tests, the owner has an absolute right to them. Hence  redistribution is illegitimate : “progressive taxation is like bonded labour,” and, echoing  Hayek , ‘social justice is a mirage’. The state must be a  minimal / night-watchman state  — protecting persons and property but with ‘no role in distributive justice’. His one exception is the  single-well  case, where a monopoly threatening life justifies intervention. Example:  Sachin Tendulkar  becoming rich because millions freely pay to watch him is perfectly just. Critique.  The theory ‘makes the welfare of the poor dependent on the justice of the rich’ and effectively defends existing oppression in the name of justice; it ignores that ‘what a person possesses is not due to talent alone’ but also to chance. The text itself judges it “just a criticism of Rawls from a libertarian point of view — not a sound theory in comparison to Rawls.” Conclusion.  Nozick powerfully defends liberty and property against Rawlsian redistribution, but by reducing the state to a guardian of holdings he leaves the disadvantaged at the mercy of the market — which is why his theory is read more as a foil to Rawls than as a self-standing account of justice. Q — Analyse Amartya Sen’s methodological critique of Rawls — social choice vs rational choice, Niti vs Nyaya, and the realization/capability approach. Gist — the spine to recall Sen accepts Rawls’ goal but rejects his method: real justice can’t be worked out by abstract people in an imaginary situation. He prefers ‘social choice’ (real people, real situations) over Rawls’ ‘rational choice’. Niti (perfect just institutions) vs Nyaya (justice as actually realised in people’s lives) — Nyaya matters more. So focus on removing real injustice and building people’s capabilities, not on designing a perfect blueprint. Model Answer Amartya Sen’s quarrel with Rawls is  methodological , not about goals. He rejects Rawls’  rational choice  — ‘abstract individuals negotiating in abstract situations’ — in favour of  social choice : ‘real persons negotiating in real-life situations’. Niti vs Nyaya.  Rawls’ ‘justice as fairness’ is  Niti  — procedural, about designing perfectly just institutions. Sen prizes  Nyaya  — a ‘realization-focused’ justice concerned with how life actually turns out. ‘Substance is more important than procedure’, so Sen’s approach is  consequentialist  where Rawls’ is deontological. He illustrates that there is no single formula with the  three children and a flute : Carla (who can play it) voices the utilitarian claim, Bob (who has no other toy) the socialist claim, and Ann (who made it) the libertarian claim — all reasonable, none absolute. In the  Krishna–Arjun  debate, Sen finds Arjun’s consequentialist worry (‘many lives would be lost’) more compelling than Krishna’s deontological ‘do your duty’. The capability approach.  Sen therefore proposes a  realization-focused capability approach : justice means expanding people’s real freedoms — ‘development as freedom’ — and removing manifest injustice, rather than chasing a perfect institutional blueprint. Conclusion.  Sen does not overthrow Rawls so much as reorient him — from ideal institutions to real lives, from arrangement to realisation. His critique makes justice comparative and practical, better suited to a diverse world where perfectly just institutions may never be agreed upon. Q — Discuss the types and dimensions of justice — distributive (David Miller), procedural vs substantive, retributive, and social/political/economic/legal. (UPSC 2018) Gist — the spine to recall Justice comes in several forms depending on what is being shared or corrected. Distributive justice = fair sharing of resources; David Miller gives 3 principles — rights, desert, and need (need is the most appropriate). Procedural justice = follow fair rules (‘procedure established by law’); substantive justice = a fair outcome (‘due process’). Also: retributive (punishment), and social/political/economic/legal justice. Model Answer Justice takes different forms depending on what is being distributed, corrected or enforced. Distributive justice  concerns the fair sharing of resources and opportunities.  David Miller  (in  Social Justice ) gives three principles, each fitting a social order: distribution by  rights  (hierarchical order — Hume), by  desert  (competitive market — Spencer), and by  need  (solidarity community — Kropotkin) — the last being ‘the most appropriate’. Schools differ: classical liberals want minimal intervention,  Nozick  almost none,  Rawls  the difference principle, and  Sen  capability-building. Procedural vs substantive justice.  Procedural justice works ‘at the level of application’ — the letter of the law, equality before law, ‘procedure established by law’ — and inspires the minimal state.  Substantive justice  cares about the  outcome  — the spirit of the law, ‘due process’ — and encourages state intervention. In India,  Maneka Gandhi  expanded Article 21 from procedure to due process, i.e. from procedural to substantive justice. Retributive justice  (rooted in Aristotle, Kant and Hegel) fixes punishment for crime; criticised for ignoring the offender, it yields to  restorative/transformative justice . Justice is also classified as  social  (equal access regardless of circumstance),  political  (power-sharing — suffrage, reservation),  economic  (equal opportunity for a dignified life) and  legal  (enforcement of established law, which ‘may or may not’ be morally just). Conclusion.  These dimensions are interlocking: legal and political justice supply the framework, while distributive and substantive justice supply the content — and the modern welfare state, guided by Rawls and Sen, tilts the balance from mere procedure toward substantive, need-based justice. Q — “Justice is an architectonic and dynamic idea.” Discuss its importance in political philosophy and how conceptions of justice have evolved. Gist — the spine to recall Justice is the ‘first virtue of social institutions’ (Rawls) — the master value the whole of political philosophy revolves around. ‘Architectonic’ = foundational; people obey institutions only if they find them just. ‘Dynamic’ = our idea of justice keeps changing — slavery, untouchability and women’s subordination were once ‘justified’, now rejected. It evolved from Plato/Aristotle → Hobbes → utilitarians → Marxists → today’s affirmative-action redistribution. Model Answer Derived from the Latin  jus  (a bond) and  jungere  (to bind), justice ‘binds people into a fair order of relationships by giving each their due’.  Rawls  calls it “the first virtue of social institutions, just as truth is of a system of thought.” Architectonic.  Justice is the  master/foundational value  around which the whole of Western political philosophy revolves —  Plato’s   Republic  is subtitled ‘concerning justice’. Its centrality is practical: people accept and obey institutions “only when they find them just”, so justice underpins political obligation and stability itself. Dynamic.  Though it embodies an ideal ‘akin to absolute truth’, our grasp of justice is ‘a continuous process’ that tracks changing  social consciousness .  D.D. Raphael  calls this ‘modern consciousness’: slavery and serfdom were once ‘justified’ in Europe, untouchability in India, the subordination of women everywhere — all now condemned. A conception of justice must therefore rest on  reason  read in the light of the prevailing social consciousness. Evolution.  Conceptions have shifted from  Plato  (one’s natural station) and  Aristotle  (proportional equality) through  Hobbes  (justice = obeying the sovereign’s order) and the  utilitarians  (the hedonistic calculus) to the  Marxists  (ending class exploitation) and, today, ‘redistribution based on affirmative action’. Conclusion.  As an architectonic idea justice is the foundation of legitimate political order; as a dynamic idea it is a moving frontier of moral progress — which is why every major theory, from Plato to Rawls and Sen, is ultimately a theory of justice. Revision Box — facts, keywords & quotes Rawls : ‘justice is the first virtue of social institutions’; justice = fairness; deontological (Kantian). Original position  +  veil of ignorance  +  maximin  → choose fair principles not knowing your place. Two principles:  (1) equal basic liberty; (2) fair equality of opportunity + difference principle (help the least advantaged) — in lexical order. Primary goods:  liberty, rights, income, wealth, self-respect. Plato : justice = each doing his own duty (station by nature);  Aristotle : treat equals equally, unequals unequally. Nozick ,  Anarchy, State and Utopia : entitlement theory (acquisition/transfer/rectification); ‘tax = forced labour’; minimal state. ‘Social justice is a mirage’ = Hayek  (not Nozick — source typo). Amartya Sen : social choice > rational choice; Niti vs Nyaya (realization-focused); three children & a flute; capability approach. Communitarians  (Sandel, Walzer, Taylor, MacIntyre): the ‘situated self’; ‘justice is the art of differentiation, not homogenisation’. Sandel ,  Liberalism and the Limits of Justice ;  Walzer ,  Spheres of Justice  (complex equality). Rawls’ reply ,  Political Liberalism : political (not metaphysical) conception; overlapping consensus (vs modus vivendi). David Miller : 3 principles of distributive justice — rights (Hume), desert (Spencer), need (Kropotkin). Procedural  (procedure established by law) vs  substantive  (due process); Maneka Gandhi expanded Art.21. The Law of Peoples : Rawls does NOT extend the difference principle between societies; ‘decent peoples’. Carole Gilligan ,  In a Different Voice : ‘ethics of care’ — justice is masculinist.
